items.title: Steve Turré interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 29, 2021
items.q: INTERVIEWER: ...you mentioned John Coltrane a little bit ago...

ctx.x: More than of a sort, it goes back to the essence of life. It’s a reflection of that. Whatever the life condition is it comes out in your music. You can’t fake that. You know we’ve all heard young students say — they’ve got a saxophone and they’ve got great fingers and they can run all the scales. I haven’t really heard any of them could play “Giant Steps” through the keys. But there’s probably a few. But they’re not playing any music. It sounds like they’re playing the computer or something. It sounds like a…

Okay. Was there a particular artist, you mentioned John Coltrane a little bit ago, and I wonder if there was a particular artist that you started listening to that was an on-spot example of what you’re talking about with the spirit, not just the technique and the instrumental prowess, but the spirit behind it?

I’ll give you a good example. My first big boss that took me around the world, Ray Charles, he had nothing but soul, nothing but soul there. No matter what he plays. He plays all kinds of music. A direct connection. Rahsaan Roland Kirk is another one. Rahsaan I first played with when I was 18 in San Francisco, before I left the Bay area, when he was in town I would play with him.
